flashcards.definition: A server disk configured so clients can access it over the network; on Windows networks, files are shared with SMB.
Centrally manages printers and print jobs across the network; it queues jobs and can hold one until the user releases it to a printer, so printouts are not left uncollected.

Stores large amounts of structured and unstructured data that can be queried for reports and used for business decisions; relational (SQL) databases, the most popular type, use tables of rows and columns.
Gives clients, usually web browsers, access to websites and web applications over HTTP or HTTPS, on the public Internet or on private intranets and extranets.
Processes email: SMTP servers deliver messages from one mail domain to another, and mailbox servers store them for the user's email client to retrieve with POP3 or IMAP.

A server that consolidates authentication for many access devices, such as switches, access points, and VPN gateways, which store no credentials and only pass them along; often run with RADIUS or TACACS+.
Lets networked systems sync their clocks to a common source so log entries have accurate time stamps; the most accurate source, an atomic clock, is Stratum 0.
A standard protocol for log collection: routers, switches, and servers send their event messages to one log collector so the logs can be reviewed in one place.
Takes a client's whole request, checks it, and forwards it to the destination server, then checks the reply; it can also filter and cache content.
A network server that uses SPF, DKIM, and DMARC to verify mail servers and filters out spoofed, malicious, or unwanted email before it reaches users' inboxes.

reference.title: Spam Gateways and Unified Threat Management

flashcards.definition: One appliance that combines the work of multiple security functions, such as firewall, intrusion prevention, anti-malware, and spam and content filtering, with simpler configuration and reporting than separate devices.

reference.title: Spam Gateways and Unified Threat Management

flashcards.definition: Spreads client requests across a farm or pool of servers that provide the same function, for high availability; it sits in front of the servers, and clients connect to its virtual server address.
A system its vendor no longer supports (end-of-life), often kept because migrating it would be too complex or expensive; with no patches coming, isolate it from the rest of the network.

An electronic device designed to perform a specific, dedicated function, such as the microcontroller in an intravenous drip-rate meter, often built for a closed network with no connection to wider data networks.
Software on ordinary computers that manages a large industrial control system (ICS) spread over many sites, gathering data from its plant equipment over WAN links.

A wearable, home appliance, vehicle, or other item equipped with sensors, software, and network connectivity, such as a smart thermostat or video doorbell; it usually needs a hub for wireless networking.
A NIC or switch interface that continually changes between up and down states; often caused by bad cabling, external interference, or a faulty NIC at the host end.
Transfers that run slower than the link should; causes include mismatched duplex settings on the network adapter and switch port, interference, a driver problem, malware, or congestion.
Interference from nearby power lines, fluorescent lighting, motors, or generators, or from a microwave oven near Wi-Fi, that slows or drops links; shielded cable reduces it on a cable run.
A Wi-Fi connection that keeps dropping; first move the devices closer together, and if they are already in range, suspect interference and adjust the channel.
Failing to join a wireless network, usually because the wrong network password was entered or the wrong security standard was selected; check the security settings on both devices.

flashcards.term: Poor VoIP (Voice over Internet Protocol) quality
flashcards.definition: Dropouts, echo, or other glitches in voice calls carried over a data network; good call quality needs QoS, with switches, access points, and routers putting voice traffic ahead of bursty data.
A signal taking too long to reach the recipient, made worse by distance and router processing delays; VoIP allows only about 150 ms one way.
The variation in delay over time, measured by sampling the time between arriving packets; usually caused by congestion on routers and switches, and VoIP buffering tolerates up to about 30 ms.
A Windows message: the host has a physical link but no DHCP lease, so it has a 169.254.x.y (APIPA) address; if many users get it, suspect the DHCP server.
